plain: bf16 is a 16-bit way of storing numbers that keeps fp32's wide range but only about three significant digits, so very small changes to a large number can disappear.
ours: With bf16 weights, a step smaller than roughly 0.2 to 0.4% of the weight is rounded to nothing. In a CPU test bf16 kept 29%, 64% and 92% of the intended weight change at learning rates of 3e-4, 1e-3 and 3e-3, so a higher learning rate can look better for a numerical reason. Schedule-Free's average is affected most. The FiLM trainer's default precision is bf16.
deeper: The 0.2 to 0.4% figure is half the spacing between neighbouring bf16 numbers (derived from the format: 7 stored fraction bits). Newton-Schulz run in bf16 is probably fine, because rounding matters when small numbers are added to large ones (weight updates, averages), and the Muon post and other implementations do it; we have not tested it ourselves and a test that logs what is lost is on our list.

options: A 16-bit number format with fp32's range but few significant digits
quiz.why: It trades precision for memory and speed.

quiz.q: A weight is 1.0 stored in bf16. A step of 0.001 (0.1%) is added. What is the likely result?
options: The weight stays 1.0, the step is rounded away
quiz.why: The step is smaller than about half the spacing between bf16 numbers near 1.0.

quiz.q: Why can bf16 make a higher learning rate look better?
options: Small steps are rounded away, so only a high rate changes anything
quiz.why: The apparent gain is numerical, not a better optimizer.

quiz.q: Is Newton-Schulz in bf16 tested in this guide?
options: No; it is probably fine, per other implementations, but we have not tested it
quiz.why: The guide says 'probably fine' and we plan to log what is lost.

plain: fp32 is the standard 32-bit number format, with about seven significant digits, so even tiny weight changes survive.
ours: Keep weights and optimizer state in fp32 if you can. In a FiLM adapter the key and value matrices moved 7 times further with fp32 state at equal loss than with bf16 state. One preliminary listen (2026-07-20) favoured fp32 over a matched bf16 twin. One later listen of full fine-tunes (2026-10-16 drone sweep) favoured bf16, but that comparison is confounded by epoch and EMA weighting. We have not compared fp32 and bf16 renders systematically by ear, so treat fp32 as safer numerically, not as automatically better to the ear.
deeper: fp32 weights cost twice the memory of 16-bit and rule out the fast attention kernels used in some runs, so on a 16 GB card it is a real trade-off. The guide recommends it for the state that accumulates small steps (weights, averages) and accepts lower precision for the heavy matrix products.

options: A 32-bit number format with about seven significant digits
quiz.why: It is the usual full-precision float.

quiz.q: Why keep weights and optimizer state in fp32?
options: Small steps survive instead of being rounded away
quiz.why: fp32 keeps small updates that bf16 would lose.

quiz.q: Does the guide claim fp32 always sounds better?
options: No; it is safer numerically, and we have not compared fp32 and bf16 systematically by ear
It says bf16 is always better
quiz.why: Numerically safer is not the same as better to the ear, and the guide says the by-ear comparison has not been done systematically.

plain: fp16 and fp8 are smaller number formats still: fp16 keeps more digits than bf16 but a narrow range, and fp8 keeps only two or three digits.
ours: We have not used either for the optimizer state in these runs. The step-size figure in guide section 4 does not show their rounding limits; section 10 covers the bf16 case that matters for us. For comparison, the smallest step that survives rounding is about half the spacing of the format: roughly 0.025 to 0.05% for fp16, 0.2 to 0.4% for bf16 and 3 to 12% for the fp8 formats.
deeper: These figures come from the formats' fraction bits (fp16 10, bf16 7, fp8 2 or 3) and are arithmetic, not measurements of our runs. fp16 overflows above about 65,000, so it needs loss scaling; fp8 is only used for the heaviest matrix products in some trainers.

quiz.q: Which format keeps the most significant digits of the three, fp16, bf16 and fp8?
quiz.why: fp16 has 10 fraction bits, bf16 has 7, fp8 has 2 or 3.

quiz.q: What is the main trade-off of fp16 compared with bf16?
options: More digits but a narrow range
Fewer digits and a wide range

quiz.q: Roughly what size of step survives in fp8 compared with the weight?
quiz.why: With only two or three fraction bits, steps below a few percent of the weight are rounded away.
